text: Τὴν ἐμοῦ κτίσιν. Emendabat qui ex Regio scripsit, κτῆσιν, quod et proclivius est. Quod tamen deest cod. quo ita emendem, placet ut κτίσιν retineam, quod sit idem ac κτίσμα, ut ea voce significet Georgius, dedisse suas ædes, et quas Alexandriæ construxerat, in quibus moniales illæ habitarent, si modo sano Ecclesiæ dogmati animum accommodarent. Videntur illæ ipsæ esse, quibus ad sanam mentem reducendis tanta Georgio navata opera, cum in Africam commeassent, de quibus in epist. ad Joann. cubicularium. Sic ægre pellem mutat Æthiops, paucique vere hæretici, quos vi quadam adegeris, nec ipsi omnino sponte, et quasi a se, confluxerint, illucente eis divini Spiritus radio, cum Ecclesiæ castra salutaverint integra in fide perseveraverint.
anchorLine: ἐμοῦ δωρηθεῖσαν ὑμῖν κτίσιν (f) ἔχειν ὑμᾶς βούλομαι·
en: On 'my creation' (ktísin): the reader who wrote 'from the Regius' emended it to ktẽsin ('possession'), which is easier. But since our codex lacks that reading, I prefer to keep ktísin, taken as the same as ktísma ('thing created'), so that by this word Georgius means he gave his own houses, including those he had built in Alexandria in which those nuns were to live, if only they would conform their minds to sound Church doctrine. These seem to be the very women for whose restoration to a sound mind Georgius did so much work when they came to Africa (see the letter to John the chamberlain). So hard is it for an Ethiopian to change his skin; and few are truly heretics, whom you might drive by some force, but who of their own accord and as if from themselves came together, with the ray of the divine Spirit shining on them, when they greeted the camps of the Church and persevered unharmed in the faith.

text: Πύῤῥον τὸν ὁσιώτατον πρεσβύτερον. Sequentem particulam, καὶ ἡγούμενον desiderant Dufrenii codex et Venet. Profusæ sane laudes, quibus hic Pyrrhum Maximus prosequitur, ejusque antistitem (et cui successor peræque sedis et hæresis fuit) Sergium; tum scilicet cum Monothelitarum hæresis semina jacerentur, jamque Alexandriæ exclusa essent Cyro ejus urbis antistite. Obtexit Sergius, quoad licuit, nec in vita palam hæreticum prodidit, quem exstinctum Joannes IV reverendæ memoriæ episcopum nuncupavit. Exinde vero Ecthéseos auctor deprehensus est, in quem Heraclius ejus crimen depulit. Male etiam habuit, quod Honorium visus est, Syra mente et fraude, trahere in communionem sui erroris, illique, pro viri simplicitate atque candore, imponere, dum contrarietatis obtentu, naturalem in Christo hominis voluntatem perimit. Excusat abunde Maximus, epistola ad Siciliæ præpositos et monachos, quam bene sanam repræsento.
anchorLine: πρεσβύτερον (g) καὶ ἡγούμενον.
en: 'Pyrrhus, the most holy presbyter.' The following phrase, 'and abbot', is lacking in Dufrenius's codex and the Venetian. Generous indeed are the praises with which Maximus here follows Pyrrhus and his bishop Sergius (whose successor was likewise in the same see and the same heresy), at a time when the seeds of the Monothelite heresy were being sown and Alexandria had already driven out Cyrus, its bishop. Sergius concealed it as far as he could, and in his lifetime did not openly show himself a heretic; after his death John IV called him a bishop 'of revered memory'. Afterwards he was found to be the author of the Ecthesis, and Heraclius cast the blame for it on him. He also behaved badly in that he was seen, with Syrian mind and deceit, to draw Honorius into communion with his error and to impose on him, in view of the man's simplicity and candour, while under the pretext of contrariety he removes the natural human will in Christ. Maximus amply excuses him in the letter to the superiors and monks of Sicily, which I give in sound form.

text: Τὴν μίαν ἐνέργειαν. Hoc itaque spectabat Pyrrhi lucubratio, ut traheret ad unius in Christo operationis assensum, Maximoque subdole obreperet, velut fere Surgius obrepsit Honorio. Scite Maximus aperiendum vocis sensum rogat, quod non raro vocibus ludant hæretici, illisque πολυσήμοις virus suum contegant ac spargant Catholico sensu, nonnihil vocibus indulgendum, uti factum Athanasio, conciliandis Orientalibus et Occidentalibus, Basilio et Gregorio Theologo erga Eunomianos, ac demum Joanni Constantinopolitano ejusque synodo, erga Philippicum: si tamen hæc postrema vera dispensatio fuit, non fidei ipsa proditio; suppressio scilicet unius et duarum in Christi operationibus et voluntatibus, ubi alterum synodo generali sic clare damnatum, alterum assertum fuerat inque dogma tractum; quam ille synodum omni conatu sublatam volebat: et vero sublatam gloriari poterat, quæsito illo silentio, quod ante decisionem exploratamque hæreticorum in eo versutiam ac fraudem, sufficiens fidei confessio videbatur, velut hic in Maximo, non post illam. Si quid tamen ibi erratum contra fidei confessionem, commune Græcorum erratum fuit, illorum etiam qui sanctitate clari in utraque Ecclesia divinis honoribus coluntur. Videnda Joannis patriarchæ Apologia ad Constantinum papam, tomo altero mei Auctarii, qui est de hæresi Monothelitarum.
anchorLine: ἐνέργειαν (h). Οὐχ ἁπλῶς γὰρ φωνὰς ἀσήμους προ-
en: On 'the one energy'. Pyrrhus's labour here aimed to draw Maximus to assent to a single operation in Christ, and to take him in by guile, as Sergius (printed 'Surgius') had imposed on Honorius. Maximus shrewdly asks that the sense of the word be made plain, because heretics often play with words and cover and spread their poison under ambiguous terms in a Catholic sense; some indulgence in words is needed, as was done for Athanasius in reconciling Easterners and Westerners, for Basil and Gregory the Theologian against the Eunomians, and finally for John of Constantinople and his synod against Philippicus, if indeed this last was a dispensation and not a betrayal of the faith: namely the suppression of one and two operations and wills in Christ, where the one had been so clearly condemned by a general synod and the other asserted and made dogma. He wanted that synod removed by every effort; and indeed it could boast of being removed, once that silence was obtained, since before the decision and the exposure of the heretics' craftiness and fraud a sufficient confession of faith seemed to exist, as here in Maximus, not after that exposure. If anything there was error against the confession of faith, it was an error common to the Greeks, even to those who are honoured with divine honours in both Churches for their holiness. See John the patriarch's Apology to Pope Constantine, in the second volume of my Auctarium, which concerns the heresy of the Monothelites.

text: Κωνσταντῖνον Σακελλάριον. Sereniss. Magni Ducis cod. exscribente Cl. V. Emerico abbate Bigotio, inscriptam habet, Πρὸς Ἰωάννην Κουβικουλάριον, ad quem plures ejus exstant epistolæ; ut erat vir in aula potens, cujus ope Maximus et Catholici indigerent: ac, num Maximus eamdem utrique epistolam miserit, cum ambo ad eum de pace scripsissent, ejusque nuntio levare senis animum studuissent; qua arrepta occasione, ita Maximus ad illos de pacis usu rescribat? Nihil certe obest ne sic dicamus, veroque similius, quam ut antiquarios, alios aliis titulos nulla ex causa mutasse existimemus. Similis item militiæ videatur uterque, et in aula militasse, alter ærario præfectus, alter sacro cubiculo; quanquam alias Σακελλάριος etiam in Ecclesiæ officiis numeretur: qua de re noster Goar, Meursius et alii. Documentis referta ad pacem bene utendam, non item dogmatica.
anchorLine: ΚΑ´. — Τοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς Κωνσταντῖνον σακελλάριον (i).
en: On 'Constantine the Sakellarios'. The codex of the Most Serene Grand Duke, as transcribed by the distinguished Abbot Emeric Bigot, has it inscribed 'To John the Koubikoularios', to whom many of his letters survive; he was a man powerful at court, whose help Maximus and the Catholics needed. And whether Maximus sent the same letter to both, when both had written to him about peace and had tried by the messenger to lift the old man's spirits, and so, seizing the occasion, replies to them about the use of peace: it surely does no harm to say so, and it is more likely than that we should suppose the antiquarii changed the titles for no reason. Both appear to have served in similar offices, both at court, one as head of the treasury, the other of the sacred bedchamber; though sakellarios is also counted among Church offices, on which our Goar, Meursius and others. The letter is full of documents (evidence) to be well used for peace, not dogmatic.

text: Ἐν τῇ καταργήσει τοῦ σώματος. Desit vox ἁμαρτίας, aut certe intelligatur; respicit enim ac reddit illud Pauli Rom. vi: Ἵνα καταργηθῇ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας· Ut destruatur corpus peccati: cui fere geminum et illud Coloss. ii: Ἐν τῇ ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκός· In exspoliatione corporis carnis, omissa voce peccatorum: quod argumento est defuisse quibusdam exemplaribus Græcis; quasi ipsum corpus, et corpus carnis, in malum sonare possint Scripturæ phrasi, ut significent opera carnalia atque vitia; sicque Maximus, non adjecta illa voce, τῆς ἁμαρτίας, scripserit. Ac quidem cod. Alexandr. τὸ, τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, laudato loco ad Col. non agnoscit, uti nec interpr. Æthiop.
anchorLine: ἐν τῇ καταργήσει τοῦ σώματος (j)
en: On 'in the destroying of the body'. The word 'of sin' is lacking, or is at least to be understood; for it looks to and reproduces Paul in Rom. 6: 'that the body of sin might be destroyed' (Ut destruatur corpus peccati), to which Col. 2 is nearly twin: 'in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh' (In expoliatione corporis carnis), the word 'of sins' being omitted. That is evidence that some Greek copies lacked it, as though 'body' itself and 'body of flesh' could in Scripture's idiom sound in a bad sense, to mean carnal works and vices; and so Maximus may have written without adding the words 'of sin'. Indeed the Alexandrian codex does not recognise 'the (words) of the sins' in the cited place of Colossians, as neither does the Ethiopic translator.

text: Πᾶσα πρὸς ἑαυτήν. Sola numeri mutatio est, sic restituto textu ex cod. Florent., nam Rom. erat, καὶ πᾶσα, quod sensum defectivum faciebat, quasi deesset πονηρία, quod et videbatur, ac crucem figebat: quibus non parcunt boni antiquarii, dum non satis attendunt, nimisque præcipitant. Refert ergo jam posita, Ἀρχάς, Ἐξουσίας, Δυνάμεις σκότους, quæ singulæ, pro animi ad eam libidine, eum sic distrahant.
anchorLine: πᾶσα πρὸς ἑαυτήν (k) διέλκουσά τε καὶ κατατέμνουσα
en: 'Every one against itself.' The only change is of number, the text being restored from the Florentine codex; for the Roman had 'and every', which made the sense defective, as though 'wickedness' were lacking, which it also appeared to be, and it fixed the cross (i.e. was a stumbling-block). The good antiquarii do not spare such readings, since they do not attend enough and are too hasty. It therefore matters that the terms already set down, 'Principalities, Powers, Powers of darkness', each of which pulls him apart according to the soul's inclination toward it.
